About

An original companion, not a copy of the book.

The dish ideas and the questions families ask came from Anya, kérek még! by Ambrus Éva, published by BOOOK Kiadó. Everything written here is new. The book’s text and photos are not reproduced.

What was kept

The feel of a Hungarian weaning kitchen: pumpkin, apple, cottage cheese, mild paprika, the occasional bit of liver, boneless fish, egg, beans, and the little party cakes families really want to bake. Where a dish was already a simple cooked fruit or vegetable, the recipe stays close to the original idea.

What was changed

No added salt or sugar for children under one. No honey anywhere. Peanut, egg, milk, wheat, sesame, fish, soy, and ground nuts are offered from around six months in a safe texture, rather than held back until the first birthday. Fried coatings are baked in the oven instead. Whole nuts, hard round pieces, carp, mustard in the early months, and salty ham have been swapped out. Each recipe page tells you whether the idea was fine as it was, adjusted, or replaced.

How the guides were written

Every claim about age, iron, protein, allergens, vitamin D, and choking is backed by a real source: ESPGHAN, WHO, EFSA, the LEAP and EAT trials, NHS, CDC, AAP, or an official Hungarian page. Where a familiar local page still teaches the old fruit-first, meat-later order, the guide points that out. This site never suggests a personal medicine dose: vitamin D for a breastfed baby is prescribed.

What this site will not do

It can’t tell you whether your child is well. It won’t walk you through back blows as if reading about them once were enough training. Take a first-aid course. If a baby goes silent and can’t cough, call for emergency help.

Inspired by Anya, kérek még! (Ambrus Éva, BOOOK Kiadó). All the text, recipes, and photos on this site are our own. This is not that book.

This is general information, not personal medical advice. Your health visitor or paediatrician knows your child. If a baby is choking, use what you learned on a first-aid course. In an emergency, call your local emergency number.
